description: Evals for the redis-docs-mcp skill: reading what the redis.io docs MCP server actually returns. Each prompt embeds the server's own instructions and tool descriptions in both arms, because in production the agent always has them - so the measured delta is the skill's guidance alone, not credit for what the tool descriptions already say. The discriminators are section-scoped ids, the metadata.version trap, and treating a search miss as non-existence.

evals.name: sections-not-pages
evals.prompt:
My agent has the redis-docs MCP server connected. Its tool inventory reads:

Server instructions: "Authoritative, up-to-date Redis documentation. Consult these tools for any question about Redis - commands, configuration, data types, clients, deployment, RediSearch/JSON, version-specific behavior - rather than answering from prior knowledge, which may be stale (Redis 8 changed several defaults and behaviors). Cite the pages you read. Start with `search`, then `fetch` the pages you need. Reserve `ask` for a question spanning several areas of the documentation at once; it takes several seconds, so prefer `search` when one page would answer."

- `search(query)`: "Search the Redis documentation by free-text query. Returns up to 8 matching pages, each with a text snippet and that page's stable `id`. This is the default tool for a Redis question. Search first, then `fetch` any `id` whose full text you need - one search plus a fetch or two answers most questions."
- `fetch(id)`: "Return the full text and metadata for one Redis documentation page: title, canonical URL, body text, and topic/version/section metadata. Takes an `id` from a `search` result or from an `ask` result's `sources`. Use it when a snippet is not enough to answer confidently, or to quote the documentation exactly."
- `ask(question)`: "Ask a natural-language question about Redis. Returns a prose answer plus the source documents behind it - any `sources[].id` can be passed to `fetch`. If the documentation does not cover the question, the answer says so. Reserve `ask` for a question spanning several areas of the documentation, where no single page answers and the parts interact - or when a `search` has come back empty or off-target. `ask` takes several seconds, so use `search` and `fetch` for anything narrower."

Debugging our integration and I think the index is broken. A search for 'hash field expiration' came back with what look like three duplicate results - same url three times. I fetched the first of those ids and got about a kilobyte of text, nowhere near the page. But when I fetched `commands/hexpire` I got the whole page, several kilobytes, examples and all. Same tool, two completely different behaviours. What is going on and do I need to work around it?
evals.expected_output: Explains the index is per-section rather than per-page: the three hits share a page url but carry distinct section ids, so they are different sections of that page rather than duplicates, and the size difference follows the id shape - a section id returns that one section while a bare page id returns the whole page. Nothing is broken; to cover the topic, fetch the other section ids the search already returned.
expectations: The output identifies that the documentation index is section-scoped rather than page-scoped.
The output explains that results sharing one url are different sections of the same page, not duplicate hits.
The output ties the size difference to the shape of the id, explaining that a section id returns one section while a bare page id such as commands/hexpire returns the whole page.
The output states that neither response is a bug, a truncation, or a misconfiguration to work around.
The output advises fetching the other section ids already present in the search results rather than re-running the search.
The output does not attribute the short response to a client-side response-size limit or a broken index.

Writing a small wrapper around these tools. To save a round trip I want to skip search entirely when I already know the page I want, and build the fetch id from the url - so `commands/setex` for https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/setex/, and by the same rule `develop/data-types/hashes` for the hashes page. I spot-checked the first one and it worked. Is this sane to build on?
evals.expected_output: Says no: ids must come from a search result or an ask result's sources rather than being constructed. Acknowledges the url-derived form happens to work for simple command pages, but explains that longer pages are addressed by section ids carrying a #sec: suffix that cannot be derived from a url, so the rule breaks exactly where the pages are big enough for the saving to matter.
expectations: The output advises against constructing fetch ids and states that valid ids come from a search result or from an ask result's sources.
The output acknowledges that the url-derived form does work for simple command pages such as commands/setex.
The output explains that longer pages are addressed by section-scoped ids carrying a #sec: suffix that cannot be derived from the url.
The output gives at least one concrete example of a section id shape the url-derived rule cannot produce, such as a named anchor or an ordinal window suffix.
The output does not endorse url-to-id construction as a general way to save a round trip.
The output offers a legitimate alternative, such as reusing ids already returned by an earlier search or by ask sources.

Reviewing a transcript. A user asked whether EXPIRE's behaviour changed in Redis 8. Our agent fetched `commands/expire`, saw `version: "1.0.0"` in the returned metadata, and answered that EXPIRE has been stable since Redis 1.0.0 with nothing new in Redis 8. Earlier in the same session it had fetched a Redis Search page whose metadata read `version: "stack"` and quietly ignored it. Was that answer sound, and what should the agent key off instead?
evals.expected_output: States the answer was unsound: on a command page metadata.version is the release the command was introduced in, not an assertion that nothing changed afterwards - and EXPIRE's own page body documents a change prior to 2.1.3 and a Redis 8 interaction with Redis Search. The 'stack' value shows the field is not even a release outside commands pages. Version questions should be answered from the page body prose and cited from there.
expectations: The output identifies metadata.version on a command page as the release the command was introduced in.
The output states that the field says nothing about behaviour changes after that release, so the agent's 'stable since 1.0.0' conclusion was unsupported.
The output notes that the EXPIRE page's own body text documents later changes, such as the pre-2.1.3 behaviour or the Redis 8 interaction with Redis Search.
The output explains that the 'stack' value is a product channel rather than a release, so the field is not uniformly a version number across the corpus.
The output directs that version-specific questions be answered from the page body prose and cited from there.
The output does not treat 1.0.0 as evidence that the command is unchanged since that release.

Post-mortem on a bad answer. A user asked our agent for the full list of keyword arguments accepted by redis-py's `ConnectionPool` constructor. The agent searched and got back `develop/clients/redis-py/connect#sec:connect-with-a-connection-pool`, `develop/clients/redis-py/async#sec:connection-pools` and `integrate/redis-py` - all about using a pool, none of them listing the constructor arguments. The agent then told the user that `max_connections` is not a real parameter. Where did it go wrong?
evals.expected_output: Identifies the error as concluding non-existence from an absent search result. Notes redis.io does index per-language client usage guides, so the hits returned were the right ones and searching was correct, but the corpus does not carry symbol-level API reference listing every constructor argument. The agent should have said the parameter is not documented on redis.io and pointed at the library's own reference or source.
expectations: The output identifies the core error as inferring that the parameter does not exist from the absence of a search result.
The output states that redis.io does index per-language client usage guides, so the pages returned were the expected ones and the search itself was not the problem.
The output states that the corpus does not carry symbol-level API reference for client libraries listing every constructor argument.
The output says the agent should have reported the parameter as not documented on redis.io rather than as not existing.
The output points to the client library's own API reference or source as where to confirm the argument.
The output does not claim that client library documentation is outside the index altogether.

evals.prompt:

If the documentation does not cover the question, the answer says so. Reserve `ask` for a question spanning several areas of the documentation, where no single page answers and the parts interact - or when a `search` has come back empty or off-target. `ask` takes several seconds, so use `search` and `fetch` for anything narrower."

Our CI agent calls `ask` once per failing test to work out whether the failure is a Redis behaviour change. Two problems. It hits rate-limit errors after a handful of calls, which makes no sense to me because it is a single process running one question at a time. And when `ask` replies that the documentation does not cover the question, the agent rephrases and retries up to three times, which mostly seems to make the first problem worse. How should this loop be built instead?
evals.expected_output: Explains the limit is per-IP - roughly four requests a minute - and shared by everything behind that address, so a single process is not the unit and other traffic from the same runner or NAT counts against it. A 'documentation does not cover this' answer is a grounded result, so rephrase-and-retry cannot help and burns the budget; fall back to search plus fetch, which draws on a separate looser budget, back off rather than retry immediately on a rate-limit error, and pass ask's sources ids to fetch for the primary source.
expectations: The output identifies the rate limit as applying per IP address, at roughly four requests per minute, rather than per process.
The output explains that the budget is shared by other traffic behind the same address, such as a CI runner or NAT, which is why a single sequential process still hits it.
The output states that a 'documentation does not cover this' answer is a grounded result, so rephrasing and retrying it cannot succeed.
The output recommends falling back to search plus fetch, noting it draws on a separate and more generous budget.
The output recommends backing off rather than retrying immediately after a rate-limit error.
The output does not recommend rephrase-and-retry as the remedy for a refusal.
